title: US Banks Post Record Second-Quarter Profits as Dealmaking Surges
summary: America's largest banks reported blockbuster second-quarter results, with JPMorgan booking a record quarterly profit and Goldman Sachs nearly doubling earnings, fueled by a wave of dealmaking and buoyant trading.
description: The largest US banks delivered exceptionally strong second-quarter results, released simultaneously on July 14, powered by a surge in dealmaking and trading activity. JPMorgan Chase reported net income of about $21.2 billion, described as the highest quarterly profit ever recorded by a US bank, with revenue and earnings well ahead of expectations. Goldman Sachs posted one of its best quarters on record, with net revenues of roughly $20.34 billion and earnings that nearly doubled from a year earlier, lifted in part by fees tied to a landmark technology-sector IPO and other high-profile transactions. Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley also beat estimates, though investors punished firms showing weaker cost control, with Citigroup and Wells Fargo shares slipping despite solid headline numbers. Executives painted a mixed macro picture: they described the US consumer as remarkably resilient while cautioning about persistent inflation, elevated asset valuations and geopolitical risk. The results arrived alongside the June inflation report and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first congressional testimony, underscoring how central bank policy and trading conditions continue to shape the sector's outlook.
image_alt: Bank headquarters representing US bank earnings (illustrative)
key_points: JPMorgan reported net income of about $21.2 billion, a record quarterly US bank profit.
Goldman Sachs posted net revenues near $20.34 billion, with earnings nearly doubling year-on-year.
All five major banks beat estimates, driven by dealmaking and trading.
Executives called the US consumer resilient but flagged inflation and valuation risks.
why_it_matters: Bank earnings are a bellwether for consumer credit, business lending and market activity, and these record results signal financial-sector strength even as executives warn about inflation and elevated valuations.

title: Fed Chair Warsh Strikes Hawkish Tone in First Congressional Testimony
summary: New Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh used his first appearances before Congress to underline a cautious, data-driven stance, reinforcing market expectations that the next rate move could be a hike rather than a cut.
description: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh reinforced a hawkish, data-dependent message in his first rounds of congressional testimony, appearing before the House Financial Services Committee around the release of the June inflation report and, days earlier, the Senate Banking Committee. Warsh emphasised the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation back to its 2% target and stopped short of signalling any near-term rate cut, keeping the benchmark federal funds rate in its current 3.50% to 3.75% range. His remarks followed a June policy meeting at which projections turned more hawkish, with nine of eighteen officials penciling in at least one rate increase before year-end and the median year-end rate projection rising to about 3.8%. Since taking the helm, Warsh has reshaped the central bank's communications, stripping out traditional forward guidance in favour of pure data dependence, and has launched several task forces to review how the Fed conducts and communicates policy. Markets have priced in a meaningfully higher chance of a rate hike at upcoming meetings, with the next decision due at the end of July, as sticky inflation and elevated oil prices keep policymakers cautious.
image_alt: Federal Reserve building representing US monetary policy (illustrative)
key_points: Warsh delivered his first testimony to the House and Senate committees in July.
He stressed a cautious, data-driven stance and gave no signal of a near-term cut.
The Fed's June projections turned hawkish, with a possible hike before year-end.
The federal funds rate remains at 3.50%-3.75% with the next decision due at end-July.
why_it_matters: The Fed chair's tone shapes expectations for mortgage, loan and savings rates, and a lean toward hikes rather than cuts affects borrowing costs for households and businesses.

title: Oil Jumps Toward $80 as Strait of Hormuz Tensions Flare Again
summary: Crude oil prices spiked toward $80 a barrel as renewed fighting around the Strait of Hormuz and a reinstated blockade on Iran revived supply fears, lifting energy stocks and complicating the inflation outlook.
description: Oil prices surged toward $80 a barrel as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz escalated once more, reviving fears about disruptions to a waterway that carries a large share of the world's seaborne crude. West Texas Intermediate spiked amid intensified confrontation between the United States and Iran over control of the strait and the reinstatement of a blockade, according to market commentary. The move made energy the best-performing sector on major North American equity benchmarks even as broader indices came under pressure from the geopolitical backdrop and questions about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence-driven rally. The renewed volatility complicates the inflation picture for central banks: higher energy costs feed directly into headline inflation and had already pushed the US consumer price index up sharply earlier in the year. Analysts cautioned that the oil market remains highly sensitive to headlines, with prices having swung between the low $70s and higher levels through 2026 depending on the state of Middle East diplomacy. A durable easing of tensions could quickly reverse the spike, while further escalation risks keeping energy prices and inflation elevated.
image_alt: Oil pumpjack representing crude oil price moves (illustrative)
key_points: Crude oil spiked toward $80 a barrel on renewed Strait of Hormuz tensions.
A reinstated blockade on Iran revived fears of supply disruption.
Energy was the top-performing sector on major North American indices.
Higher oil prices complicate the inflation outlook for central banks.
why_it_matters: Oil price swings feed directly into fuel costs and inflation, influencing central bank decisions and the prices households pay for energy, transport and goods.

title: Fairfax and Emirates NBD Submit Revised Bids for India's IDBI Bank
summary: India's government has received revised financial bids from Fairfax Financial and Emirates NBD for a controlling 60.72% stake in state-linked IDBI Bank, moving the long-running privatisation closer to completion.
description: India's long-delayed sale of IDBI Bank has moved a step closer, with the government receiving revised financial bids from Canada's Fairfax Financial and the UAE's Emirates NBD for a controlling 60.72% stake in the lender. The stake is being sold jointly by the central government and Life Insurance Corporation of India, and the transaction is one of the country's most closely watched privatisations. Both bidders had earlier cleared regulatory scrutiny, including the Reserve Bank of India's 'fit and proper' assessment and security clearances, before submitting updated offers following due diligence. A successful sale would mark a significant milestone in the government's broader disinvestment agenda and would hand a substantial Indian banking franchise to a foreign strategic owner, subject to final regulatory approvals. For the winning bidder, IDBI offers an established branch network and customer base, while for the government the deal would unlock capital and reduce state ownership in the banking sector. The revised bids set the stage for the authorities to evaluate valuations and move toward selecting a preferred buyer, though the timeline for a final decision and completion will depend on further clearances.
image_alt: Bank documents representing a stake sale process (illustrative)
key_points: The government received revised bids from Fairfax Financial and Emirates NBD for IDBI Bank.
The sale covers a controlling 60.72% stake held by the government and LIC.
Both bidders earlier cleared RBI 'fit and proper' and security checks.
A completed deal would be a major milestone in India's privatisation agenda.
why_it_matters: The IDBI sale is a landmark test of India's bank privatisation drive, and foreign ownership of a major lender could reshape competition and capital in the sector.

title: Indian Banks Pitch M&A Financing to Corporates After RBI Eases Rules
summary: Indian banks are marketing acquisition financing to corporate clients following new Reserve Bank of India norms, setting up sharper competition with private credit funds for a fast-growing lending opportunity.
description: Indian banks are actively pitching mergers-and-acquisitions financing to corporate clients after the Reserve Bank of India introduced new norms allowing them to lend against acquisitions, opening a business long dominated by private credit funds and offshore lenders. The rule change permits banks to finance corporate takeovers under defined conditions, giving domestic lenders a foothold in a lucrative segment as deal activity picks up. Bankers see the shift as a chance to deepen relationships with large corporate borrowers and to compete on price and speed with alternative credit providers that had filled the gap while banks were restricted. The move aligns with a broader deepening of India's credit markets: analysts have flagged that India Inc is expected to require tens of trillions of rupees in debt funding over the coming years to support the country's long-term growth ambitions, and a wider debt capital market is seen as essential. For banks, acquisition financing offers higher-yielding lending opportunities, though it also brings added credit and concentration risks that supervisors will monitor. The development signals growing competition between traditional lenders and the rapidly expanding private credit industry in India.
image_alt: Indian rupee notes representing corporate lending (illustrative)
key_points: New RBI norms let Indian banks finance corporate acquisitions.
Banks are pitching M&A financing to corporates, competing with private credit funds.
India Inc is expected to need large debt funding over coming years.
The segment offers higher yields but adds credit and concentration risks.
why_it_matters: Allowing banks into acquisition financing reshapes India's corporate lending landscape, intensifying competition with private credit and expanding funding options for dealmaking companies.

title: Bank of Korea Raises Rates for First Time in Over Three Years
summary: The Bank of Korea lifted its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 2.75% on July 16, its first increase since January 2023, and signalled further tightening as inflation, housing prices and household debt stay elevated.
description: The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in more than three years, lifting the base rate by a quarter percentage point to 2.75% on July 16 in a unanimous decision. The move reversed an easing cycle that had begun in October 2024 and ended 14 consecutive months without a change, marking the bank's first hike since January 2023. Governor Shin Hyun-song, who took charge of the central bank in late April, said policymakers acted decisively against inflation, which the bank expects to remain above its 2% target through 2027, and warned that housing prices and household debt remain elevated. Two forces drove the decision: global oil prices climbing on Middle East tensions and feeding through to energy costs, and a resilient export sector, led by semiconductors, that has supported domestic demand. The bank also revised up its 2026 growth forecast. Shin signalled that further increases could follow but declined to commit to a timetable, saying the bank was keeping all options open and would respond to incoming data. The decision runs counter to the broader global drift toward rate cuts.
image_alt: Seoul cityscape representing South Korea's monetary policy (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Korea raised its base rate to 2.75% on July 16, its first hike since January 2023.
The unanimous decision reversed an easing cycle begun in October 2024.
Governor Shin cited inflation, elevated housing prices and household debt.
The bank signalled further tightening but gave no fixed timetable.
why_it_matters: South Korea's shift back to rate hikes bucks the global easing trend and raises borrowing costs for households already carrying high debt, while reflecting inflation pressure from energy and strong exports.

title: Bank of England Says Financial System Resilient but Flags Rising Risks
summary: The Bank of England's July Financial Stability Report judged the UK financial system resilient despite Middle East-driven volatility, while warning about rising equity-market leverage, private credit and AI-related operational risks.
description: The Bank of England concluded that the UK financial system has remained resilient despite the macroeconomic shock from the Middle East conflict, in its July Financial Stability Report published on July 7. The central bank said banks are well capitalised and that households and businesses show aggregate strength, leaving the core of the system able to absorb shocks. At the same time, it flagged a set of growing vulnerabilities: rising leverage in equity markets, risks building in private credit, and emerging operational risks from frontier artificial intelligence models. The report urged firms to act on a joint statement issued earlier in the year by the Bank, the Financial Conduct Authority and the Treasury on frontier AI, and to strengthen cyber and operational resilience, including through work on the UK's critical third-party regime. It also noted that the energy-driven supply shock had pushed market interest rates higher across advanced economies and lifted government bond yields. The assessment comes with inflation running at 2.8% and the Bank having held its base rate at 3.75%, with its next monetary policy decision scheduled for July 30 amid persistent cost pressures and geopolitical uncertainty.
image_alt: Bank of England building representing UK financial stability (illustrative)
key_points: The July Financial Stability Report judged the UK system resilient despite Middle East volatility.
It flagged rising equity-market leverage, private credit and AI-related operational risks.
Firms were urged to strengthen cyber and operational resilience.
Inflation stood at 2.8%, with the next rate decision due July 30.
why_it_matters: The central bank's stability assessment shapes how banks and lenders manage risk, and its warnings on AI and private credit signal areas where consumers and the wider economy could be exposed.

title: Bank of Japan Holds Above Ceasefire Optimism as Nikkei Hits Records
summary: Japanese equities pushed to record highs in July, buoyed by optimism over easing Middle East tensions and a chip-led rally, after the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1% in June and signalled more tightening ahead.
description: Japanese equities extended their advance to record highs in July, supported by optimism over easing Middle East tensions and strength in technology and semiconductor shares. The Nikkei's rally followed the Bank of Japan's June decision to raise its policy rate by a quarter point to 1%, its highest level in about three decades, as the central bank judged that upside risks to inflation had grown while downside risks from the regional conflict had faded. Investors have interpreted the combination of firm corporate earnings, a weaker yen at points during the year and resilient global demand for Japanese exports as supportive of equities, even as higher rates raise borrowing costs. The central bank has signalled a continued tightening bias, with policymakers pointing toward a gradual move over time toward a more neutral setting, and markets are watching upcoming meetings for the timing of the next step. The record-setting run in Japanese stocks stands in contrast to more cautious sentiment elsewhere in Asia, where weak data weighed on some markets, and reflects growing confidence that Japan's exit from ultra-low interest rates can proceed without derailing growth.
image_alt: Tokyo skyline representing Japanese equity markets (illustrative)
key_points: The Nikkei pushed to record highs in July on ceasefire optimism and a chip rally.
The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1% in June, a multi-decade high.
The bank signalled a continued gradual tightening bias.
Japanese gains contrasted with weaker sentiment elsewhere in Asia.
why_it_matters: Japan's record equity run and gradual rate normalisation influence the yen, global bond markets and investor flows, with implications for borrowing costs and portfolios worldwide.

title: Singapore Proposes Protected Cell Company Framework to Boost Risk Transfer
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore has opened a consultation on a Protected Cell Company framework that would let a single legal entity ring-fence assets and liabilities across cells, supporting captive insurance and insurance-linked securities.
description: The Monetary Authority of Singapore has launched a consultation on a Protected Cell Company framework designed to scale alternative risk-transfer solutions such as captive insurance, insurance-linked securities and sovereign risk pools. Announced by MAS chairman and deputy prime minister Gan Kim Yong in late June and opened for feedback on July 7 until August 7, the structure would operate as a single legal entity with a central 'Core' and one or more 'Cells', with the assets and liabilities of each cell legally segregated from the others and from the core. MAS said existing arrangements require a separate legal entity, such as a special purpose vehicle, for each programme, and that the associated cost and effort can deter adoption; the cell structure aims to lower those barriers. The framework would be open to MAS-licensed entities carrying out captive insurance, insurance-linked securities and sovereign risk pools, reinforcing Singapore's position as a leading reinsurance and risk-transfer hub in Asia. Officials acknowledged that structural reform alone cannot resolve deeper demand-side barriers, such as affordability, awareness and thin local risk capital, that have kept captive ownership among Asian parents relatively low. The consultation invites industry views before the framework is finalised.
image_alt: Singapore skyline representing its insurance and reinsurance hub (illustrative)
key_points: MAS opened a consultation on a Protected Cell Company framework, running July 7 to August 7.
The structure ring-fences assets and liabilities across cells within one legal entity.
It targets captive insurance, insurance-linked securities and sovereign risk pools.
MAS said it aims to cut the cost and effort of setting up separate vehicles.
why_it_matters: The framework could make it cheaper and simpler to set up alternative risk-transfer structures, strengthening Singapore's role as a regional reinsurance hub and expanding options for insuring complex risks.

title: MAS and Industry Set Out Safeguards for Autonomous AI Agents in Finance
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore, working with banks and fintechs, has released a white paper proposing guardrails for autonomous AI agents that perform financial tasks, as human oversight becomes harder to maintain at scale.
description: The Monetary Authority of Singapore, together with banks and fintech partners, has released a white paper setting out an industry framework to keep autonomous artificial-intelligence agents in finance operating safely, securely and within defined risk limits. The paper responds to the rapid emergence of AI agents that can carry out financial tasks with limited human intervention, a shift that makes continuous human oversight impractical as deployment scales. It proposes runtime safeguards and governance measures intended to ensure such agents behave predictably, stay within authorised boundaries and can be monitored, controlled and, where necessary, halted. The initiative reflects Singapore's broader strategy of encouraging financial innovation while managing the associated operational, security and accountability risks, and complements the regulator's wider work on technology risk, cyber resilience and AI governance. By convening industry participants to agree common principles, MAS aims to give firms a practical reference point for adopting agentic AI responsibly rather than leaving each institution to devise its own approach. The framework signals growing supervisory attention to the risks posed by increasingly autonomous systems across banking, payments and asset management, an area regulators worldwide are beginning to scrutinise.
image_alt: AI and digital systems representing autonomous agents in finance (illustrative)
key_points: MAS and industry partners released a white paper on governing autonomous AI agents in finance.
It sets out runtime safeguards as human oversight becomes impractical at scale.
The framework aims to keep agents within defined risk limits and under control.
It complements MAS work on technology risk, cyber resilience and AI governance.
why_it_matters: As AI agents take on more financial tasks, clear safeguards help protect consumers and the system from errors and misuse, and could shape how regulators worldwide approach agentic AI.

title: UAE's Emirates NBD Advances in Race for India's IDBI Bank
summary: Dubai's Emirates NBD has submitted a revised bid for a controlling stake in India's IDBI Bank, underscoring Gulf lenders' push to expand in fast-growing South Asian markets.
description: Emirates NBD, one of the largest banking groups in the UAE, has advanced in the contest for India's IDBI Bank after submitting a revised financial bid for a controlling 60.72% stake alongside Canada's Fairfax Financial. The Dubai-based lender's pursuit of a major Indian franchise reflects a broader strategy among Gulf banks to expand beyond home markets into large, fast-growing economies, and would give Emirates NBD a substantial retail and corporate presence in India if successful. The bidder had earlier cleared regulatory scrutiny, including India's central bank assessment and security clearances, before updating its offer following due diligence. For the UAE banking sector, a successful acquisition would mark one of its most significant outbound investments in Indian financial services and deepen economic ties between the two countries, which have strengthened commercial links in recent years. The transaction still requires the Indian government to evaluate the revised bids and select a preferred buyer, with completion subject to final regulatory approvals. The outcome will be closely watched as a signal of Gulf lenders' appetite for cross-border banking deals and of India's willingness to admit foreign strategic owners into its banking system.
image_alt: Dubai skyline representing UAE banking expansion (illustrative)
key_points: Emirates NBD submitted a revised bid for a controlling stake in India's IDBI Bank.
It is competing with Canada's Fairfax Financial for the 60.72% stake.
The lender earlier cleared Indian regulatory and security checks.
A deal would be a major outbound investment for the UAE banking sector.
why_it_matters: The bid highlights Gulf banks' ambitions in South Asia and, if successful, would deepen UAE-India financial ties while testing India's openness to foreign ownership of major lenders.

title: Volkswagen Turnaround in Focus as July 24 Earnings Loom
summary: Volkswagen's shares have slid to their lowest level in years as the German carmaker prepares to report earnings on July 24, with investors seeking clarity on plant closures, job cuts and mounting Chinese competition.
description: Volkswagen enters its July 24 earnings report under intense pressure, with its shares having fallen to their lowest level in more than a decade amid a mountain of challenges. The German group faces soaring competition from Chinese electric-vehicle brands, a costly restructuring and questions about its strategy, and reports earlier in the year pointed to potential major layoffs and plant closures. Any restructuring is complicated by the influence of unions and the state of Lower Saxony, which holds a significant stake, as well as legal constraints on closing plants. The company is also said to be winding down an autonomous-vehicle unit into which it had poured billions of euros. The upcoming results give management a chance to explain its turnaround plan and provide guidance at a time when short-sellers have circled the stock. Volkswagen's difficulties are emblematic of a wider strain across Germany's auto sector, a cornerstone of the country's economy, as legacy manufacturers grapple with the transition to electric vehicles, higher costs and the loss of market share in China. Investors will scrutinise the outlook for margins, cost cuts and the group's competitive position in its most important markets.
image_alt: Car manufacturing line representing Volkswagen's challenges (illustrative)
key_points: Volkswagen shares have fallen to their lowest in more than a decade ahead of July 24 earnings.
The group faces intense Chinese EV competition and a costly restructuring.
Reports point to potential layoffs, plant closures and winding down an autonomous unit.
Investors want clarity on the turnaround plan and margin guidance.
why_it_matters: Volkswagen is a pillar of Germany's economy, so its struggles carry wide implications for jobs, suppliers and Europe's auto industry as it confronts Chinese competition and the EV transition.

title: APRA's New Longevity Capital Rules Take Effect to Support Retirement Income
summary: Australia's prudential regulator has implemented finalised changes to the capital treatment of longevity products from July 1, aiming to make lifetime-income products more attractive for insurers to offer and improve retirement outcomes.
description: Australia's prudential regulator has brought into effect finalised changes to the way insurers must hold capital against longevity products, with the reforms taking effect on July 1. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority said the changes are designed to improve retirement outcomes by making it more feasible for life insurers to offer lifetime-income products that protect retirees against the risk of outliving their savings. Longevity products, such as annuities and other guaranteed-income solutions, have historically been capital-intensive for insurers, which can limit supply and choice for retirees. By recalibrating the capital treatment, including through an adjusted illiquidity premium approach, APRA aims to better align capital requirements with the underlying risks and encourage a broader market for these products. To support implementation, the regulator released a reporting template for insurers choosing to use the new approach. The reforms come as Australia's retirement system, built around compulsory superannuation, increasingly focuses on helping members convert their savings into reliable income in retirement rather than simply accumulating balances. APRA supervises institutions holding trillions of dollars in assets for depositors, policyholders and superannuation members, and the change forms part of its broader push to strengthen retirement provision.
image_alt: Retirement planning documents representing lifetime-income products (illustrative)
key_points: APRA's revised capital treatment of longevity products took effect on July 1.
The changes aim to make lifetime-income products easier for insurers to offer.
Longevity products protect retirees against outliving their savings.
APRA released a reporting template to support insurers using the new approach.
why_it_matters: Easier capital treatment could expand the availability of guaranteed retirement-income products, helping Australians turn superannuation savings into reliable income and manage the risk of outliving their money.

title: RBI's UDGAM Portal Expands to Help Indians Reclaim Dormant Deposits
summary: The Reserve Bank of India's UDGAM portal now lets people track old savings accounts, fixed deposits and other inactive holdings in one place, aiming to make it easier to recover unclaimed money across banks and insurers.
description: The Reserve Bank of India has expanded its UDGAM portal to help individuals track and reclaim dormant financial holdings, including old savings accounts, fixed deposits, recurring deposits and other inactive accounts, from a single online platform. The portal is designed to simplify access to otherwise scattered financial information and help people recover unclaimed amounts that may have been lying idle for years across banks, insurers and capital-market intermediaries. By consolidating this information, the initiative aims to improve transparency, strengthen financial inclusion and remove the complicated procedures that previously discouraged people from pursuing dormant funds. Large sums accumulate in India's financial system each year as accounts fall inactive after account holders move, forget details or die without nominees claiming the money, and regulators have pushed to return these amounts to their rightful owners. The move is part of a broader effort by the RBI and the government to improve consumer protection and grievance handling in the financial sector, with the central bank also urging institutions to strengthen internal complaint-resolution processes. For households, the expanded portal offers a practical route to identify and recover money they may not even realise they are owed.
image_alt: Person checking finances online representing dormant deposit recovery (illustrative)
key_points: The RBI's UDGAM portal now tracks dormant savings accounts, fixed and recurring deposits.
It consolidates scattered account information to help recover unclaimed funds.
The aim is greater transparency and stronger financial inclusion.
It is part of a wider push to improve consumer protection and grievance handling.
why_it_matters: The portal gives ordinary savers a simpler way to find and reclaim money lying dormant across banks and insurers, potentially returning significant unclaimed sums to their rightful owners.

title: US Credit Card Arrears Climb as Consumers Feel Strain of High Rates
summary: The share of US credit card accounts in arrears has risen quickly to around 13%, according to Bank of England data, signalling growing strain on American consumers after an extended stretch of high borrowing costs.
description: Signs of strain are building among US consumers as the proportion of credit card accounts in arrears has climbed markedly, reaching around 13% in the first quarter of 2026, according to analysis cited in the Bank of England's July Financial Stability Report. The report noted that the share of US consumer credit loans more than 90 days in arrears has increased significantly over the past three years, with credit card delinquencies rising particularly quickly. It offered some reassurance, however, observing that the share of accounts in arrears but not yet written off, a more relevant gauge of potential future losses for lenders, had levelled off at around 4% at the end of 2025, near its long-run average. The data point to the cumulative pressure on households from an extended period of elevated interest rates, even as headline measures of consumer spending have remained resilient and bank executives describe the American consumer as broadly healthy. Delinquency and charge-off rates on credit cards and auto loans are being closely watched as indicators of whether borrowers are reaching their limits. Rising arrears could eventually weigh on lending, consumer spending and the broader economy if the trend continues.
image_alt: Credit cards representing consumer debt and arrears (illustrative)
key_points: The share of US credit card accounts in arrears rose to around 13% in Q1 2026.
Consumer loans more than 90 days in arrears have climbed over three years.
Accounts in arrears but not yet written off levelled off near 4%, close to the long-run average.
Delinquency trends are a key gauge of consumer strain from high interest rates.
why_it_matters: Rising credit card arrears signal that high borrowing costs are pressuring US households, a trend that could eventually curb spending and lending and weigh on the broader economy.
